newsitem.title: USA: Crime-lab tests back serial bomber theory in Atlanta.
newsitem.headline: Crime-lab tests back serial bomber theory in Atlanta.

text.p: Federal investigators, who have believed for months that a serial bomber could be on the loose in Atlanta, now have hard crime-lab evidence to support their suspicions, sources close to the investigations said Thursday.

Extensive lab tests conducted at a U.S. Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco and Firearms (ATF) crime lab in Atlanta and at an FBI facility in Washington showed that bomb components from attacks an abortion clinic and a gay nightclub were identical.
The sources said results also showed that shrapnel used in those two attacks and last July's Centennial Olympic Park bombing originated in the same foundry.
Spokesmen for the FBI and the ATF had no comment Friday.

Meanwhile, federal investigators were expected to hold a news conference in Atlanta next week to discuss changes in the structure of investigating force and to ask the general public for further assistance in tracking down those responsible for the bombings.
The Olympic bomb, which exploded during a crowded outdoor concert at the height of the games, left two people dead and more than 100 injured.
While the abortion clinic bombing in January and the nightclub bombing a month later killed no one, the two explosions injured at least a dozen people.

Investigators said the new forensic evidence does not lead to a final conclusion about how many assailants were behind the bombings. But it has made a serial bomber far more likely and heightened fears of another strike.
One investigator said authorities believe they are dealing with an extremist cell influenced by a violent rightwing millennialist theology.
An anonymous letter purported to be from a shadowy anti-abortion group called the Army of God claimed responsibility for the abortion clinic and nightclub bombings.
In copies mailed to news organisations including Reuters, the letters' author divulged details about the makeup of bombs used in the attacks and invited FBI experts to confirm them.
Although the letter was mailed about 12 hours after the nightclub bombing, investigators said the information it contained was not specific enough to be convincing.
Altogether five bombs exploded in Atlanta between last July and February.
Unlike the Olympic bombing, the abortion clinic and nightclub attacks each involved a second "sucker" bomb apparently intended for law enforcement agents and emergency workers.
